Closing the Sim2Real Performance Gap in RL

Akhil S Anand    Shambhuraj Sawant    Jasper Hoffmann    Dirk Reinhardt    Sebastien Gros
Abstract

Sim2Real aims at training policies in high-fidelity simulation environments and effectively transferring them to the real world. Despite the developments of accurate simulators and Sim2Real RL approaches, the policies trained purely in simulation often suffer significant performance drops when deployed in real environments. This drop is referred to as the Sim2Real performance gap. Current Sim2Real RL methods optimize the simulator accuracy and variability as proxies for real-world performance. However, these metrics do not necessarily correlate with the real-world performance of the policy as established theoretically and empirically in the literature. We propose a novel framework to address this issue by directly adapting the simulator parameters based on real-world performance. We frame this problem as a bi-level RL framework: the inner-level RL trains a policy purely in simulation, and the outer-level RL adapts the simulation model and in-sim reward parameters to maximize real-world performance of the in-sim policy. We derive and validate in simple examples the mathematical tools needed to develop bi-level RL algorithms that close the Sim2Real performance gap.

1 Introduction

Sim2Real rl (rl) addresses the challenge of obtaining real-world data by training rl agents in simulation and then transferring them to real-world environments (Talvitie, 2018). The overarching objective of Sim2Real rl is to train agents capable of achieving optimal real-world performance, which we refer to as Sim2Real optimality. Sim2real rl has been supported by significant advances in capabilities and fidelity of simulators (Makoviychuk et al., 2021; Todorov et al., 2012; Collins et al., 2021). Despite these advances, the inevitable discrepancies between simulated and real-world conditions lead to a significant performance gap upon policy transfer, often referred to as the Sim2Real gap (Da et al., 2025). To mitigate this gap, methods such as domain randomization (Tobin et al., 2017; Zhao et al., 2020) or domain adaptation (Höfer et al., 2021) are used to ensure that the agent is robust to distribution shifts that occur while transferring to the real world. However, robustness does not yield Sim2Real optimality (Zhou et al., 1996).

Sim2Real rl methods typically do not directly optimize policy performance for the real-world conditions; instead, they rely on proxies such as simulator accuracy, parameter variability, or prediction fidelity (Da et al., 2025). However, the conditions required for Sim2Real optimality are distinct from conditions on simulator accuracy or robustness (Skelton, 1989; Anand et al., 2024). Consequently, these methods cannot inherently guarantee optimal real-world performance. The Sim2Real performance gap in rl is closely tied to the objective mismatch in mbrl (mbrl) (Wei et al., 2024; Eysenbach et al., 2022; Janner et al., 2019), emphasizing that standard metrics for prediction accuracy in simulation models often fail to correlate with the real-world performance of the policy developed in simulation. In theory, for any stochastic real-world system, it is possible to adjust the simulation environment such that the optimal policy in simulation is also optimal in the real world (Anand et al., 2025).

However, there is still no general consensus on the correct objective for training the simulation model, beyond the intuitive goal that both the learned model and policy should ultimately optimize the expected return in the real-world environment (Wei et al., 2024). Following previous works (Anand et al., 2025; Nikishin et al., 2022; Amos and Yarats, 2020), we frame the problem of finding or adapting the simulation environment parameters that will guarantee Sim2Real optimality, and cast it as an rl problem on the real environment data. This forms a bi-level rl framework, where the inner-level consists of a standard in-simulation rl agent, and the outer-level comprises a real-world rl agent that updates the simulator parameters by evaluating the real-world performance of the in-sim agent.

In this paper, we consider the general case where the rl agent in simulation is obtained through spg (spg) methods, considering it is generalizable to both discrete and continuous action spaces. To that extent, we derive the mathematical tools that serve as the foundation for bi-level policy gradient rl algorithms that can achieve Sim2Real optimality both in Sim2Real rl and dyna-style mbrl frameworks. The central contribution is the estimation of sensitivities of the in-sim rl process using spg.

2 Related Work

Sim2Real RL Approaches:

The problem of the Sim2Real gap has been traditionally addressed by either enriching the simulator fidelity or exposing agents to diverse simulated scenarios. Domain randomization is a common approach that perturbs the simulator parameters during training to improve robustness, such that the resulting in-sim policy generalizes better to the real-world (Tobin et al., 2017; Duan et al., 2024). Such approaches often demand extensive domain knowledge and manual feature engineering. Few works have explored automated curriculum-based randomization to reduce manual tuning (Akkaya et al., 2019; Yuan et al., 2024). In another approach, domain adaptation rather than randomizing aligns feature or parameter distributions between the simulator and real environment, commonly via adversarial training on observations (Chen et al., 2020; Long et al., 2018; Pei et al., 2018; Höfer et al., 2021). In meta rl, the agent is trained on a distribution of environments with the goal that the agent can then quickly adapt to the real environment Finn et al. (2017); Brown et al. (2020). Here, the environment distribution during training needs to be carefully designed such that it covers the real-world environment during testing. Other approaches include grounded action methods to adjust simulator dynamics to match observed real trajectories (Hanna and Stone, 2017; Desai et al., 2020) and distributionally robust rl formulates the problem as maximizing worst-case returns under bounded transition shifts (Liu and Xu, 2024). Recently, llm have been used to improve simulator predictions in a zero-shot fashion (Da et al., 2024).

Most Sim2Real rl approaches are robustness-focused rather than performance-oriented; they seek to reduce the Sim2Real performance gap by optimizing for proxy objectives (e.g., simulator accuracy, variability) rather than the real-world performance directly (Da et al., 2025). As a result, they can improve stability under distribution shift but do not offer a guarantee on optimal performance. Few works have explored embedding task performance in domain adaptation. For example, RL-CycleGAN fine-tunes scene parameters by minimizing an rl-consistency loss on a learned Q-function (Rao et al., 2020), yet this is an indirect surrogate for real-world performance. In contrast, our approach focuses purely on optimality and couples the domain adaptation directly with the real-world performance of the in-sim policy. We achieve this by casting domain adaptation as a bi-level rl problem, where the outer-level rl directly optimizes simulator parameters to maximize real-world performance.

Objective Mismatch in mbrl:

Objective mismatch is a well-recognized problem in mbrl (Lambert et al., 2020; Eysenbach et al., 2022; Janner et al., 2019). An overview of a broad class of decision-aware mbrl approaches that aim to solve this problem is provided in (Wei et al., 2024). Value-based learning is a prominent decision-aware mbrl approach which seeks models that reproduce equivalent value functions instead of state transitions of the environment, following the (Proper) Value Equivalence Principle (Grimm et al., 2020; Grimm et al., 2021). In line with this, value-aware modeling methods (Farahmand et al., 2017) use the Bellman error in the model updates. Empirical evidence further underscores the issue, demonstrating a substantial Sim2Real performance gap due to objective mismatch across various frameworks (Hansen et al., 2022; Farahmand et al., 2017; Schrittwieser et al., 2020; Wan et al., 2024; Voelcker et al., 2023). In contrast to value-based methods, the category of policy-based methods considers the real-world policy gradient as the most important feedback signal to adapt the simulation environment. An approach in this direction is using a modified reward signal that guides the parameter updates of the simulation environment in a direction such that the policy gradient in the simulator reproduces the real-world policy gradient (Jia et al., 2024). Similar other approaches update the model such that the resulting distance between the respective policy gradients is minimized in the ℓ2\ell_{2} or ℓq\ell_{q} norm (D’Oro et al., 2020; Abachi et al., 2021).

Differentiable Planning is another class of policy-based methods where the model-based policy-optimization process is embedded in a differentiable program to jointly optimize policy and model towards the same objective Wei et al. (2024). The approach we take in this paper can be categorized as policy-based differentiable planning. Works in this direction include the Differentiable Cross Entropy Method (Amos and Yarats, 2020) or the Optimal Model Design (Nikishin et al., 2022), which proposes implicit differentiation of the Bellman operator to identify performance-oriented models through gradient-based optimization. The work presented here can be seen as an extension of (Nikishin et al., 2022), where the in-sim policy is assumed to be a softmax of a learned Q-function allowing to tune the policy by implicit differentiation of the Bellman equation of the Q-function. Instead, in this work we highlight the possibility of the implicit differentiation of the spg (spg), without assuming a specific structure of the policy. In general, model-based implicit functions has been proposed in the machine learning literature Amos et al. (2018), which is theoretically and practically justified by the mpc (mpc) community (Gros and Zanon, 2019; Reiter et al., 2025).

3 Preliminaries

3.1 Reinforcement Learning and Optimal Decision-Making

rl is a framework for sequential decision-making where an agent interacts with an environment to maximize cumulative rewards (Sutton and Barto, 2018). Formally, an rl problem is defined as a mdp (mdp), (𝒮,𝒜,𝒫,r,γ)(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},\mathcal{P},r,\gamma), where 𝒮\mathcal{S} is the state space, 𝒜\mathcal{A} is the action space, 𝒫⁡(s′|s,a)\mathcal{P}(s^{\prime}|s,a) is the real-world transition model defining the probability of transitioning to state s′s^{\prime} given s,as,a. r:𝒮×𝒜→ℝr:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\to\mathbb{R} is the scalar reward function provided by the environment, γ∈[0,1]\gamma\in[0,1] is the discount factor. A policy π⁡(a|s)\pi(a|s) defines the agent’s behavior, mapping states to a distribution over actions. The objective of rl is to find the optimal policy π⋆\pi^{\star} that maximizes the expected return: J⁡(π)=𝔼τ∼π​[∑t=0∞γt​r​(st,at)]{J(\pi)=\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim\pi}\left[\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^{t}r(s_{t},a_{t})\right]}. The state-value function and action-value function are defined as: Vπ(s)=𝔼π[∑t=0∞γtr(st,at)∣s0=s],Qπ(s,a)=𝔼π[∑t=0∞γtr(st,at)∣s0=s,a0=a]{V^{\pi}(s)=\mathbb{E}_{\pi}\left[\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^{t}r(s_{t},a_{t})\mid s_{0}=s\right],}\,{Q^{\pi}(s,a)=\mathbb{E}_{\pi}\left[\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^{t}r(s_{t},a_{t})\mid s_{0}=s,a_{0}=a\right]}. The optimal value function V⋆​(s)V^{\star}(s) and optimal Q-function Q⋆​(s,a)Q^{\star}(s,a) satisfy the Bellman optimality conditions: V⋆​(s)=maxa⁡Q⋆​(s,a),Q⋆​(s,a)=r⁡(s,a)+γ​𝔼s′∼𝒫​[V⋆​(s′)]V^{\star}(s)=\max_{a}Q^{\star}(s,a),\,Q^{\star}(s,a)=r(s,a)+\gamma\mathbb{E}_{s^{\prime}\sim\mathcal{P}}\left[V^{\star}(s^{\prime})\right]. The optimal policy satisfies: π⋆​(s)=arg⁡maxa​Q⋆​(s,a)\pi^{\star}(s)=\arg\max_{a}Q^{\star}(s,a).

3.2 In-sim Reinforcement Learning

We consider a simulation environment as a abstract function fθf_{\theta}, approximating the real-world distribution 𝒫\mathcal{P}, used to generate the next state given a current state-action pair

s′∼fθ(.∣s,a).s^{\prime}\sim f_{\theta}(.\mid s,a). (1)

and used to generate simulation-based trajectories mimicking the real system. The θ\theta may include the parameters of the mathematical function representing the simulator dynamics, such as ode, dnn, etc. We consider a reward function Rθ​(s,a)R_{\theta}(s,a) in the simulation as a model of the real-world reward rr. The parameters of RθR_{\theta} and fθf_{\theta} together constitute what we refer to as simulator parameters. The in-sim policy πϕ\pi_{\phi} is an implicit function of simulator parameters θ\theta through fθf_{\theta} and RθR_{\theta}, derived by solving the in-sim rl problem:

πϕ⋆=arg⁡maxϕ​𝔼st,at∼πϕ,fθ​[∑t=0∞γt​Rθ​(st,at)|s0=s].\pi_{\phi^{\star}}=\arg\max_{\phi}\mathbb{E}_{s_{t},a_{t}\sim\pi_{\phi},f_{\theta}}\left[\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^{t}R_{\theta}(s_{t},a_{t})\Bigm|s_{0}=s\right]. (2)

The optimality of the πϕ⋆\pi_{\phi^{\star}} can be established through the Bellman equations: Vθ⋆​(s)=maxa⁡Qθ⋆​(s,a),Qθ⋆​(s,a)=Rθ​(s,a)+γ​𝔼s′∼fθ​[Vθ⋆​(s′)],and​πϕ⋆​(s)=arg⁡maxa​Qθ⋆​(s,a)V^{\star}_{\theta}(s)=\max_{a}Q^{\star}_{\theta}(s,a),\,Q^{\star}_{\theta}(s,a)=R_{\theta}(s,a)+\gamma\mathbb{E}_{s^{\prime}\sim f_{\theta}}[V^{\star}_{\theta}(s^{\prime})],\,\text{and}\,\pi_{\phi^{\star}}(s)=\arg\max_{a}Q^{\star}_{\theta}(s,a). Note that the objects Vθ,QθV_{\theta},Q_{\theta} and πϕ\pi_{\phi} are implicitly defined by fθf_{\theta} and RθR_{\theta}.

4 Optimal Sim2Real RL

In this section, we establish the notion of Sim2Real Optimality and describe how it can be realized. We consider a real-world mdp as defined in Section 3.1, and its approximation as an in-sim mdp described in Section 3.2. Assuming the real-world and in-sim mdp share the same state-space 𝒮\mathcal{S} and have a unique optimal policy, the in-sim mdp achieves Sim2Real optimality if the optimal policy obtained in simulation is also optimal for the real-world environment, i.e., πϕ⋆=π⋆\pi_{\phi^{\star}}=\pi^{\star}. This can be expressed as the necessary and sufficient optimality condition:

arg​maxa​Qθ⋆​(s,a)=arg​maxa​Q⋆​(s,a),∀s.\mathrm{arg}\max_{{a}}\,Q_{\theta}^{\star}({s},{a})=\mathrm{arg}\max_{{a}}\,Q^{\star}({s},{a}),\quad\forall\,{s}\,. (3)

Sim2Real optimality is critical in applications where real-world performance is the priority. Conventionally, the performance objective is pursued indirectly by constructing highly accurate models of real-world dynamics within the simulation environments, for example, through supervised learning. However, for stochastic systems, the prediction accuracy of the simulation model does not necessarily correlate with the real-world performance of the resulting in-sim policy (Anand et al., 2025). This stems from the near-impossibility of perfectly replicating the complex conditional distributions that govern real-world dynamics in simulation (Ljung, 1999). However, it has been shown that even an in-sim policy under an imperfect simulation model fθf_{\theta} can achieve Sim2Real optimality under specific conditions on the model or on the in-sim reward function (Anand et al., 2024; Gros and Zanon, 2019).

To close the Sim2Real performance gap, we propose framing the identification of the optimal simulator parameters θ⋆\theta^{\star} satisfying the necessary condition for Sim2Real optimality in (3) as a policy gradient rl problem:

θ⋆∈arg⁡maxθ⋆​𝔼τ∼πϕ⋆,𝒫​[∑t=0∞γt​r​(st,at)]s.t.(2).\theta^{\star}\in\arg\max_{\theta^{\star}}\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim\pi^{\star}_{\phi},\mathcal{P}}\left[\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^{t}r(s_{t},a_{t})\right]\,\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\eqref{eq:pi_phi}\,. (4)

The rl formulations in (2) and (4) together constitute a bi-level rl. The inner level constitutes the in-sim rl problem to derive πϕ⋆\pi_{\phi^{\star}} which is implicitly defined by fθf_{\theta} and RθR_{\theta} (2). Upon deployment in the real-world environment, policy πϕ\pi_{\phi} generates real transition data (s,a,s+,r)(s,a,s_{+},r). The outer-level rl then adapts the simulator dynamics fθf_{\theta} and reward function RθR_{\theta} to optimize real-world policy performance under the real-world transition data. Note that the outer-level rl does not fit the simulator parameters to mimic real-world dynamics, but instead optimizes them to maximize the performance of the policy implicitly defined by these parameters. Additionally, the solution θ⋆\theta^{\star} to (4) is not unique, allowing the selection of simulator parameters aligned with the real-world dynamics according to a user-specified loss function ℒ⁡(⋅)\mathcal{L}(\cdot) as follows:

θ⋆=arg​minθ⁡ℒ​(fθ,ρ,Rθ,r),s.t.(4)∀s,a.{{\theta}^{\star}}=\argmin_{\theta}\,\,\mathcal{L}\left(f_{\theta},\rho;\,R_{\theta},r\right),\quad\mathrm{s.t.}\quad\eqref{eq:bi_level_rl}\quad\forall\,s,a\,. (5)

mle (mle), Bayesian estimation, or expected-value losses are common choices of ℒ⁡(⋅)\mathcal{L}(\cdot).

4.1 Stochastic Policy Gradient for Bi-level RL

In this section, we will derive the mathematical tools to solve problem (4). For generality across continuous and discrete state-action domains and stochastic simulation models, we consider the case that both the in-sim and real-world rl agents are trained using spg. Consider the spg of the in-sim rl:

φ^​(ϕ,θ)\displaystyle\hat{\varphi}(\phi,\theta) =𝔼s∼ρ^θπϕ​[∇ϕ​log​πϕ​(a|s)​Q^θπϕ​(s,a)],\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{s\sim\hat{\rho}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}}}[\nabla_{\phi}\log\pi_{\phi}(a|s)\hat{Q}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}}(s,a)]\,, (6)

where Q^θπϕ\hat{Q}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}} is the critic of policy πϕ\pi_{\phi} as seen by the simulations, and ρ^θπϕ\hat{\rho}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}} is the simulated discounted Markov chain density associated to policy πϕ\pi_{\phi} under the model fθf_{\theta}. Under local convergence, i.e., φ^​(ϕ,θ)=0{\hat{\varphi}(\phi,\theta)=0}, spg provides a locally optimal policy πϕ\pi_{\phi}. We consider this locally converged ϕ\phi in the rest of our analysis, thereby formulating the optimal bi-level rl problem (4) as:

θ⋆=arg⁡maxθ​𝔼τ∼πϕ,𝒫​[∑t=0∞γt​r​(st,at)]s.t.φ^​(ϕ,θ)=0.\theta^{\star}=\arg\max_{\theta}\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim\pi_{\phi},\mathcal{P}}\left[\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^{t}r(s_{t},a_{t})\right]\,\quad\text{s.t.}\quad{\hat{\varphi}(\phi,\theta)=0}\,. (7)

Given φ^​(ϕ,θ)=0{\hat{\varphi}(\phi,\theta)=0}, it implicitly defines ϕ\phi as a function of θ\theta. Therefore, the sensitivity of the in-sim policy parameters ϕ\phi with respect to the simulator parameters θ\theta can be given by the ift (ift) (Krantz and Parks, 2002),

∇θϕ=−(∇ϕφ^​(ϕ,θ))−1​∇θφ^​(ϕ,θ).\nabla_{\theta}\phi\;=\;-\,\bigl(\nabla_{\phi}\hat{\varphi}\bigl(\phi,\theta\bigr)\bigr)^{-1}\,\nabla_{\theta}\hat{\varphi}\bigl(\phi,\theta\bigr)\,. (8)

Note that there exist iterative methods and their approximation to invert the Jacobian term ∇ϕφ^​(ϕ,θ)\nabla_{\phi}\hat{\varphi}\bigl(\phi,\theta\bigr) (Liesen and Strakos, 2013; Yang et al., 2024). Using ∇θϕ\nabla_{\theta}\phi, we can then formulate solution to (7) as the outer-level spg using the the real-world transition data:

φ⁡(ϕ,θ)\displaystyle\varphi\bigl(\phi,\theta\bigr) =𝔼s∼ρπϕ​[∇θ​log​πϕ​(a∣s)​Qπϕ​(s,a)],\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{s\sim\rho^{\pi_{\phi}}}\Bigl[\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\phi}(a\mid s)\,Q^{\pi_{\phi}}(s,a)\Bigr], (9a)
∇θ​log​πϕ​(a∣s)\displaystyle\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\phi}(a\mid s) =∇θϕ​∇ϕ​log⁡πϕ​(a∣s),\displaystyle=\nabla_{\theta}\phi\;\nabla_{\phi}\log\pi_{\phi}(a\mid s)\,, (9b)

where QπϕQ^{\pi_{\phi}} is the critic of in-sim policy πϕ\pi_{\phi} as seen by the real world, ρπϕ\rho^{\pi_{\phi}} is the discounted Markov chain density resulting from using in-sim policy πϕ\pi_{\phi} in the real world, and (9b) is result of chain-rule with ift condition. To update the simulation parameters via (9a), we must compute the sensitivity of the in-sim rl solution with respect to the simulation parameters, represented by the gradient ∇θϕ\nabla_{\theta}\phi. Computing ∇θϕ\nabla_{\theta}\phi is the only additional component of (9a) compared to the classic spg. We now introduce two lemmas that will help us compute ∇θϕ\nabla_{\theta}\phi and derive the full expression for the real-world spg in (9a). Note that the ∂\partial in Lemma 1 and Lemma 2 denotes either the partial derivative with respect to ϕ\phi or θ\theta.

Lemma 1 (Sensitivity of a Markov Chain).

Sensitivity of the expected value operation of a function η⁡(sk,ak)\eta(s_{k},a_{k}) under a Markov chain induced by policy πϕ\pi_{\phi} under the transition model fθf_{\theta} is given by:

∂𝔼s∼ρ^θ,kπϕ​[η⁡(sk,ak)]=𝔼s0∼ρ0,ai∼πϕ,si+1∼fθπϕ​[η⁡(sk,ak)​(∂log⁡πϕ​(ak∣sk)+∑i=0k−1∂log⁡fθπϕ​(si+1∣si,ai))].\displaystyle\partial\,\mathbb{E}_{s\sim\hat{\rho}_{\theta,k}^{\pi_{\phi}}}\bigl[\eta(s_{k},a_{k})\bigr]=\mathbb{E}_{\begin{subarray}{c}s_{0}\sim\rho^{0},\,a_{i}\sim\pi_{\phi},\\ s_{i+1}\sim f^{\pi_{\phi}}_{\theta}\end{subarray}}\Bigl[\,\eta(s_{k},a_{k})\,\Bigl(\partial\log\pi_{\phi}(a_{k}\!\mid\!s_{k})+\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}\partial\log f^{\pi_{\phi}}_{\theta}(s_{i+1}\!\mid\!s_{i},a_{i})\Bigr)\Bigr]\,. (10)

Given the Bellman conditions,

∂Qπ​(s,a)\displaystyle\partial Q^{\pi}(s,a) =∂R⁡(s,a)+γ​𝔼s+∼f​[∂Vπ​(s+)+Vπ​(s+)​∂log⁡f⁡(s+|s,a)],\displaystyle=\partial R(s,a)+\gamma\mathbb{E}_{s_{+}\sim f}\left[\partial V^{\pi}(s_{+})+V^{\pi}(s_{+})\partial\log f(s_{+}|s,a)\right], (11a)

With the help of these two Lemmas, we now present the spg theorem for the bi-level rl problem.

Theorem 1 (Sensitivity of in-sim spg).

Given a simulation model fθf_{\theta}, reward function RθR_{\theta}, and a resulting in-sim policy πϕ\pi_{\phi} optimal in its parameter (i.e., φ^​(ϕ,θ)=0{\hat{\varphi}(\phi,\theta)=0}), the sensitivity of the in-sim policy parameters ϕ\phi w.r.t. to the simulation model and reward parameters θ\theta is given by:

∇θϕ\displaystyle\nabla_{\theta}\phi =−(𝔼s∼ρ^θπϕ​[∇ϕ​ϕ​log​πϕ​Q^θπϕ+∇ϕ​log​πϕ​∇ϕQ^θπϕ]⏟Gradient​of​φ^​w.r.t.ϕ+∇ϕ𝔼s∼ρ^θπϕ​[∇ϕ​log​πϕ​Q^θπϕ]⏟Gradient​of​dist.ρ^θπϕ​w.r.t.ϕ)−1\displaystyle=-\Bigl(\underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{s\sim\hat{\rho}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}}}\bigl[\nabla_{\phi\phi}\log\pi_{\phi}\,\hat{Q}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}}+\nabla_{\phi}\log\pi_{\phi}\,\nabla_{\phi}\hat{Q}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}}\bigr]}_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathrm{Gradient\,of\,}\hat{\varphi}\mathrm{\,w.r.t.\,}\phi\end{subarray}}\;+\;\underbrace{\nabla_{\phi}\mathbb{E}_{s\sim\hat{\rho}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}}}\bigl[\nabla_{\phi}\log\pi_{\phi}\,\hat{Q}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}}\bigr]}_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathrm{Gradient\,of\,dist.\,}\hat{\rho}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}}\mathrm{\,w.r.t.\,}\phi\end{subarray}}\Bigr)^{-1}
(𝔼s∼ρ^θπϕ​[∇ϕ​log​πϕ​∇θQ^θπϕ]⏟Gradient​of​φ^​w.r.t.θ+∇θ𝔼s∼ρ^θπϕ​[∇ϕ​log​πϕ​Q^θπϕ]⏟Gradient​of​dist.ρ^θπϕ​w.r.t.θ).\displaystyle\qquad\qquad\Bigl(\underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{s\sim\hat{\rho}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}}}\bigl[\nabla_{\phi}\log\pi_{\phi}\,\nabla_{\theta}\hat{Q}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}}\bigr]}_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathrm{Gradient\,of\,}\hat{\varphi}\mathrm{\,w.r.t.\,}\theta\end{subarray}}\;+\;\underbrace{\nabla_{\theta}\mathbb{E}_{s\sim\hat{\rho}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}}}\bigl[\nabla_{\phi}\log\pi_{\phi}\,\hat{Q}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}}\bigr]}_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathrm{Gradient\,of\,dist.\,}\hat{\rho}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}}\mathrm{\,w.r.t.\,}\theta\end{subarray}}\Bigr). (12)

In (12), the terms ∇ϕ​log​πϕ\nabla_{\phi}\log\pi_{\phi}, ∇ϕ​ϕ​log​πϕ\nabla_{\phi\phi}\log\pi_{\phi} are the gradient and hessian of the in-sim policy w.r.t to its parameters. The critic sensitivity term, ∇θQ^θπϕ\nabla_{\theta}\hat{Q}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}} is the influence of changing the reward and model parameters θ\theta on the simulation-based critic under a fixed policy πϕ\pi_{\phi}, given by the recursions:

∇θQ^θπϕ​(s,a)\displaystyle\nabla_{\theta}\hat{Q}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}}(s,a) =∇θRθ​(s,a)+γ​𝔼s+∼fθ​[∇θV^θπϕ​(s+)+V^θπϕ​(s+)​∇θ​log⁡fθ​(s+|s,a)],\displaystyle=\nabla_{\theta}R_{\theta}(s,a)+\gamma\mathbb{E}_{s_{+}\sim f_{\theta}}\left[\nabla_{\theta}\hat{V}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}}(s_{+})+\hat{V}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}}(s_{+})\nabla_{\theta}\log f_{\theta}(s_{+}|s,a)\right], (13a)
∇θV^θπϕ​(s)\displaystyle\nabla_{\theta}\hat{V}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}}(s) =𝔼a∼πϕ​[∇θQ^θπϕ​(s,a)].\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi_{\phi}}\left[\nabla_{\theta}\hat{Q}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}}(s,a)\right]\,. (13b)

The second critic sensitivity term, ∇ϕQ^θπϕ\nabla_{\phi}\hat{Q}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}} is the influence of changing the policy parameters ϕ\phi on the simulation-based critic under a fixed reward RθR_{\theta} and model fθf_{\theta}, given by:

∇ϕQ^θπϕ​(s,a)\displaystyle\nabla_{\phi}\hat{Q}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}}(s,a) =γ​𝔼s+∼fθ​[∇ϕV^θπϕ​(s+)],\displaystyle=\gamma\mathbb{E}_{s_{+}\sim f_{\theta}}\left[\nabla_{\phi}\hat{V}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}}(s_{+})\right], (14a)
∇ϕV^θπϕ​(s)\displaystyle\nabla_{\phi}\hat{V}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}}(s) =𝔼a∼πϕ​[∇ϕQ^θπϕ​(s,a)+Q^θπϕ​(s,a)​∇ϕ​log⁡πϕ​(a|s)].\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi_{\phi}}\left[\nabla_{\phi}\hat{Q}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}}(s,a)+\hat{Q}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}}(s,a)\,\nabla_{\phi}\log\pi_{\phi}(a|s)\right]\,. (14b)

Both critic sensitivities (13) and (14) can be approximated iteratively using function approximation or for each of the samples separately. In practice, all components in Theorem 1 will be estimated from the in-sim transition data (s^,a,s^+,R)(\hat{s},a,\hat{s}_{+},R) be evaluated from a model sampling. Let us label Let(s0j,a0j,R0j​…,sNj,aNj,Rnj)(s_{0}^{j},a_{0}^{j},R_{0}^{j}\ldots,s_{N}^{j},a_{N}^{j},R_{n}^{j}) be the sampled trajectory j∈{1,…,n}j\in\left\{1,\ldots,n\right\} of length NN. The expected value approximation of the Markov Chain sensitivity of the in-sim policy gradient w.r.t θ\theta and ϕ\phi is given by:

∇ϕ𝔼s∼ρ^θπϕ[∇ϕlogπϕQ^θπϕ]≈1n​N∑k=0N∑j=1n\displaystyle{\nabla_{\phi}}\mathbb{E}_{s\sim\hat{\rho}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}}}\left[\nabla_{\phi}\log\pi_{\phi}\,\hat{Q}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}}\right]\approx\frac{1}{nN}\sum_{k=0}^{N}\sum_{j=1}^{n} ∇ϕlogπϕ(akj|skj)Q^θπϕ(skj,akj)\displaystyle\nabla_{\phi}\log\pi_{\phi}\left(\left.a^{j}_{k}\right|s^{j}_{k}\right)\,\hat{Q}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}}\left(s_{k}^{j},a_{k}^{j}\right)
⊗(Wϕ,kj+∇ϕlogπϕ(akj|skj))\displaystyle\otimes\left(W_{\phi,k}^{j}+\nabla_{\phi}\log\pi_{\phi}\left(\left.a_{k}^{j}\right|s_{k}^{j}\right)\right) (15)

where: ⊗\otimes represents outer product and Wϕ,0j=0;W^{j}_{\phi,0}=0;  Wϕ,kj=Wϕ,k−1j+∇ϕlogπϕ(ak−1j|sk−1j)W_{\phi,k}^{j}=W_{\phi,k-1}^{j}+\nabla_{\phi}\log\pi_{\phi}\left(\left.a^{j}_{k-1}\right|s^{j}_{k-1}\right). Similarly,

∇θ𝔼s∼ρ^θπϕ[∇ϕlogπϕQ^θπϕ]≈1n​N∑k=0N∑j=1n\displaystyle\nabla_{\theta}\mathbb{E}_{s\sim\hat{\rho}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}}}\left[\nabla_{\phi}\log\pi_{\phi}\,\hat{Q}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}}\right]\approx\frac{1}{nN}\sum_{k=0}^{N}\sum_{j=1}^{n} ∇ϕlogπϕ(akj|skj)Q^θπϕ(skj,akj)⊗Wθ,kj\displaystyle\nabla_{\phi}\log\pi_{\phi}\left(\left.a^{j}_{k}\right|s^{j}_{k}\right)\,\hat{Q}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}}\left(s_{k}^{j},a_{k}^{j}\right)\otimes W_{\theta,k}^{j} (16)

where: Wθ,0j=0W^{j}_{\theta,0}=0 and Wθ,kj=Wθ,k−1j+∇θlogfθ(skj|sk−1j,ak−1j)W_{\theta,k}^{j}=W_{\theta,k-1}^{j}+{\nabla_{\theta}}\log f_{\theta}\left(\left.s^{j}_{k}\right|s^{j}_{k-1},a^{j}_{k-1}\right). A high-level algorithmic description of the bi-level rl framework is provided in Algorithm 1.

5 Illustrative Examples

We present two concrete, illustrative realizations of the bi-level rl framework: (i) stochastic control in a discrete state-action space, and (ii) stochastic continuous control with linear dynamics. Note that the goal of this illustration is to validate the sensitivity estimate (12) by evaluating the outer-level spg updates. Since both problems are simple to solve, we employ exact methods to derive the in-sim stochastic policies: dp (dp) in case (i) and lqr (lqr) in case (ii). These exact policies naturally satisfy the convergence condition for the spg: φ^​(ϕ,θ)=0{\hat{\varphi}(\phi,\theta)=0}. In both cases, we initialize five distinct simulation environments with parameters randomly sampled around the real-world environment parameters. During the bi-level rl training, both the simulation and reward parameters are iteratively updated as described in Algorithm 1, until convergence. The training progress of the outer-level rl is shown in Fig. 3. The convergence of outer-level rl in Fig. 3 serves as a validation to sensitivity estimation in Theorem 1

Discrete MDP:

We consider a stochastic discrete MDP with state set 𝒮={s0,s1,s2}\mathcal{S}=\{s_{0},s_{1},s_{2}\} and action set 𝒜={𝚜𝚝𝚊𝚢=𝟶,𝚖𝚘𝚟𝚎=𝟷}\mathcal{A}=\{\mathtt{stay=0},\mathtt{move=1}\}, so each action may yield different successor states. The state-transition model includes the parameters: θs,af=(θs,a,0f,θs,a,1f,θs,a,2f)∈ℝ3{\theta^{f}_{s,a}=(\theta^{f}_{s,a,0},\theta^{f}_{s,a,1},\theta^{f}_{s,a,2})\in\mathbb{R}^{3}} via fθ​(s′∣s,a)=softmax​(θs,af)s′{\displaystyle f_{\theta}(s^{\prime}\mid s,a)=\mathrm{softmax}(\theta^{f}_{s,a})_{s^{\prime}}}. Rewards use θR∈ℝ3×2\theta^{R}\in\mathbb{R}^{3\times 2} via Rθ​(s,a)=θs,aRR_{\theta}(s,a)=\theta^{R}_{s,a}. In this example, we use dp to compute exact solutions of a discrete in-sim policy and its value function. This discrete policy is converted to a stochastic policy that uses action preferences (logits) hϕ​(s,a)=ϕs,aπ{\displaystyle h_{\phi}(s,a)=\phi^{\pi}_{s,a}}, i.e., the learnable score for action aa in state ss, with θπ∈ℝ3×2{\theta^{\pi}\in\mathbb{R}^{3\times 2}}. The policy selects actions by πθ​(a∣s)=softmax​(hθ​(s,⋅))a{\displaystyle\pi_{\theta}(a\mid s)=\mathrm{softmax}\bigl(h_{\theta}(s,\cdot)\bigr)_{a}}. Then we estimate the critic sensitivity (13) and (14) in a tabular form iteratively until convergence using on-policy in-sim data. We use the same in-sim on policy data to estimate the Markov chain sensitivities (15) and (16).

Continuous MDP:

We consider a parameterized linear system with additive Gaussian noise; s+=θs​s+θa​a+ϵ,ϵ∼𝒩⁡(0,σ2){s_{+}=\theta_{s}\,s+\theta_{a}\,a+\epsilon,\quad\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2})} and a parameterized exponential reward function Rθ​(s,a)=exp⁡(−λ⁡(θq​s2+θr​a2)){R_{\theta}(s,a)\;=\;\exp\left(-\lambda\bigl(\theta_{q}\,s^{2}\;+\;\theta_{r}\,a^{2}\bigr)\right)}. The real system parameters are: θs=1,θa=1,θq=1,θr=1{\theta_{s}=1,\;\theta_{a}=1,\;\theta_{q}=1,\;\theta_{r}=1}. The simulation model and reward parameters are chosen randomly between 00 and 11. In this example, we solve the in-sim policy and value function exactly using lqr, and then use nn to approximate them. By approximating them with nn, we can validate the robustness of the sensitivity estimates with regards to the noisy nn predictions. Then we estimate the critic sensitivity (13) and (14) for each sample iteratively until convergence using in-sim data under the nn policy. We use the same in-sim on-policy data to estimate the Markov chain sensitivities (15) and (16).

6 Discussions

This paper presents a general mathematical framework for bi-level rl using an implicit differentiation of in-sim spg, see Theorem 1, for Sim2Real approaches. Using such sensitivities can achieve local optimality of Sim2Real rl and dyna-style mbrl settings. By estimating the optimal simulator parameters with outer-level rl, we can exploit a full suite of rl techniques in simulation, including domain randomization, to develop a policy that is optimal for the real world. In contrast, simply fine-tuning a policy that was learned in simulation on real-world data does not afford this flexibility. Moreover, learning an optimal simulation model provides valuable insights into which scenarios drive decision-making in practice, thereby enhancing explainability. Indeed, industrial practitioners often strictly prefer in-sim optimization over fine-tuning the policy separately for the reasons outlined above. Moreover, fine-tuning the in-sim reward parameters provides extra flexibility in closing the Sim2Real performance gap.

Since the simulation model parameters typically obtained via classical model-fitting approaches (Ljung, 1995) approximate the real world dynamics with reasonable accuracy, the optimal simulator parameters likely lie within a neighbourhood of those estimates. Consequently, in practice, the outer-level rl can be implemented as a local search on the simulator parameter space (Grudic and Ungar, 2000) similar to (Jia et al., 2024). Additionally, the parameter search space in Sim2Real rl is often not large, since practitioners would prefer to modify only a small set of simulator parameters. Indeed, Sim2Real optimality can be achieved by adapting only the reward parameters while keeping the simulation model parameters fixed (Gros and Zanon, 2019). Moreover, initializing the outer-loop critic with the in-sim critic could accelerate convergence of the outer-loop rl (Yin et al., 2025).

Although Theorem 1 assumes the learning of the in-sim policy has fully converged to local optimality, in practice, a not-fully-converged in-sim policy only perturbs the already noisy real-world gradient of the outer-level rl. Therefore, inner-level rl not converging is a concern only when the outer-level solution is close to optimal and requires accurate gradients. However, in that situation the simulator-parameter updates are naturally small, making it easier for the in-sim policy to converge.

The bi-level rl framework is applicable to any in-sim policy optimization scheme, provided one can estimate the sensitivity of the in-sim policy with respect to the simulator parameters. Notable examples include bi-level rl schemes for mpc (Reiter et al., 2025), and cem (cem) (Amos and Yarats, 2020; Wan et al., 2024). Consequently, the key contribution of the framework presented in this paper is the sensitivity analysis of the spg-based rl used to train the in-sim policy. This extends the previous work of Nikishin et al. (2022) that assumed that the policy is derived from a Q-function via a softmax allowing to derive a model gradient by implicit differentiation of the Bellman equations. The bi-level rl framework is directly applicable to dyna-style mbrl settings, where dynamics model and reward functions typically learned for prediction accuracy can be adapted by an outer-level rl loop to improve the real-world performance (4).

The sensitivity analysis in Theorem 1 could be incorporated into standard rl algorithms such as ppo (ppo) (Schulman et al., 2017) and sac (sac) (Haarnoja et al., 2018) with the addition of differentiating extra terms in their policy gradient equations without additional complexity. Given the challenges inherent in real-world online learning, offline rl is a suitable and promising framework for the outer-level rl algorithms. Such algorithmic development is a natural and promising avenue for future work.

6.1 Limitations

While this paper presents a mathematical framework and proof of concept for the bi-level rl, additional algorithmic development is needed to develop a scalable bi-level rl algorithm that can be used by Sim2Real rl practitioners. The practical deployment will require the development of specific bi-level rl algorithms based on the results of Section 4. Moreover, the proposed bi-level rl framework is computationally expensive, due to the estimation of the critic sensitivities(13) and of the optimal in-sim policy (14) with respect to the simulation parameters. Since, in practice, these sensitivities need to be approximated using dnn, the computational burden increases significantly with the size of in-sim policy parameters. Therefore, efficient approximations of the critic sensitivities are required to make the framework efficiently scalable to larger problems.

While bi-level rl accounts for the aleatoric uncertainties in the real-world environment, it does not account for the epistemic uncertainties. However, in real-world decision-making problems, epistemic uncertainty can significantly impact the value function estimates, leading to issues such as overestimation. To address this, epistemic uncertainties must be managed using probabilistic models of dynamics, or by penalizing the in-sim selection of out-of-distribution state-action pairs (Kidambi et al., 2020).

One key assumption in our framework is that the simulator and the real system share the same state representation. While this assumption simplifies the analysis, real-world environments often provide only partial or noisy observations (e.g., images or sensor readings). Therefore, extending the bi-level rl to work directly with the observation space is an important direction for future work.

The bi-level rl framework requires the dynamics model and reward functions in the simulation to be differentiable and sufficiently smooth for accurate sensitivity estimates. Although this may seem limiting, differentiable simulators are rapidly becoming standard, including domains with discrete state or action spaces and applications such as contact robotics, where dynamics are inherently discontinuous (Newbury et al., 2024). In the case of mbrl, when both dynamics and reward functions are parameterized by neural networks, they are inherently differentiable.

7 Conclusion

The bi-level rl framework provides a principled method for closing the Sim2Real performance gap, which is essential for deploying rl in real-world environments. In contrast to existing Sim2Real rl approaches that optimize the simulator fidelity or inject variability as indirect proxies for real-world performance, the bi-level rl framework performs objective-oriented adaptation of simulator parameters driven directly by real-world policy performance. It aligns simulator adaptation with the true performance objective and, in theory, achieves Sim2Real optimality. Similarly, the bi-level rl framework overcomes the objective-mismatch issue in mbrl by directly coupling model learning to real-world performance, rather than relying on indirect criteria. While this paper establishes the theoretical foundations and mathematical tools for bi-level rl, algorithmic developments are necessary to implement this approach in large-scale rl problems. Advancements in simulation environments, such as differentiable simulators and gpu (gpu) acceleration, will be critical to scaling the bi-level rl framework for practical deployment.

Appendix A Proof of Theorem 1, Lemma 1, and Lemma 2

Here we provide the proof for lemma 1, lemma 2, and theorem 1. We consider the stochastic policy gradient:

φ^​(ϕ,θ)=𝔼s∼ρ^θπϕ​[∇ϕ​log​πϕ​Q^θπϕ]\displaystyle\hat{\varphi}\left(\phi,\theta\right)=\mathbb{E}_{s\sim\hat{\rho}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}}}\left[\nabla_{\phi}\log\pi_{\phi}\hat{Q}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}}\right] (17)

where ϕ\phi are the policy parameters, θ\theta are the parameters attached to the model and cost in the simulation-based training environment, and Q^θπϕ\hat{Q}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}} is the critic of policy πϕ\pi_{\phi} as seen by the simulations. Distribution ρ^θπϕ\hat{\rho}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}} is the simulated “discounted Markov chain density" associated to policy πϕ\pi_{\phi}. Assuming that the simulation-based policy training sets the policy parameters ϕ\phi such that (17) is zero, ϕ\phi becomes an implicit function of θ\theta.

The real-world (outer-level) policy gradient reads as:

φ⁡(ϕ,θ)\displaystyle\varphi\left(\phi,\theta\right) =𝔼s∼ρπϕ​[∇θ​log​πϕ​Qπϕ]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{s\sim\rho^{\pi_{\phi}}}\left[\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\phi}Q^{\pi_{\phi}}\right] (18)

where QπϕQ^{\pi_{\phi}} is the critic of policy πϕ\pi_{\phi} as seen by the real world, and ρπϕ\rho^{\pi_{\phi}} is the “discounted Markov chain density” resulting from using policy πϕ\pi_{\phi} in the real world. Here, θ\theta implicitly affects log⁡πϕ\log\pi_{\phi}, as any changes in θ\theta would change the local optima for the inner loop resulting in a different policy πϕ\pi_{\phi}, hence, we have,

φ⁡(ϕ,θ)\displaystyle\varphi\left(\phi,\theta\right) =𝔼s∼ρπϕ​[∇θϕ​∇ϕ​log⁡πϕ​Qπϕ]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{s\sim\rho^{\pi_{\phi}}}\left[\nabla_{\theta}\phi\nabla_{\phi}\log\pi_{\phi}Q^{\pi_{\phi}}\right] (19)

The key element to compute the world policy gradient is to find the sensitivity ∇θϕ\nabla_{\theta}\phi using φ^​(ϕ,θ)=0\hat{\varphi}\left(\phi,\theta\right)=0. The IFT readily applies (under some conditions), and

∇ϕφ^​∇θϕ+∇θφ^\displaystyle\nabla_{\phi}\hat{\varphi}\nabla_{\theta}\phi+\nabla_{\theta}\hat{\varphi} =0\displaystyle=0 (20)
∇ϕθ\displaystyle\nabla_{\phi}\theta =−∇ϕφ^−1​∇θφ^\displaystyle=-\nabla_{\phi}\hat{\varphi}^{-1}\nabla_{\theta}\hat{\varphi} (21)

Sensitivities ∇θφ^,∇ϕφ^\nabla_{\theta}\hat{\varphi},\,\nabla_{\phi}\hat{\varphi} can be computed as:

∇θφ^\displaystyle\nabla_{\theta}\hat{\varphi} =𝔼s∼ρ^θπϕ​[∇ϕ​log​πϕ​∇θQ^θπϕ]+∇θ𝔼s∼ρ^θπϕ​[∇ϕ​log​πϕ​Q^θπϕ]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{s\sim\hat{\rho}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}}}\left[\nabla_{\phi}\log\pi_{\phi}\nabla_{\theta}\hat{Q}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}}\right]+\nabla_{\theta}\mathbb{E}_{s\sim\hat{\rho}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}}}\left[\nabla_{\phi}\log\pi_{\phi}\,\hat{Q}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}}\right] (22a)
∇ϕφ^\displaystyle\nabla_{\phi}\hat{\varphi} =𝔼s∼ρ^θπϕ​[∇ϕ​ϕ​log​πϕ​Q^θπϕ+∇ϕ​log​πϕ​∇ϕQ^θπϕ]+∇ϕ𝔼s∼ρ^θπϕ​[∇ϕ​log​πϕ​Q^θπϕ]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{s\sim\hat{\rho}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}}}\left[\nabla_{\phi\phi}\log\pi_{\phi}\hat{Q}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}}+\nabla_{\phi}\log\pi_{\phi}\nabla_{\phi}\hat{Q}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}}\right]+\nabla_{\phi}\mathbb{E}_{s\sim\hat{\rho}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}}}\left[\nabla_{\phi}\log\pi_{\phi}\,\hat{Q}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}}\right] (22b)

where:

  • •

    ∇ϕ​ϕ​log​πϕ\nabla_{\phi\phi}\log\pi_{\phi} is an explicit expression from the policy function

  • •

    ∇θQ^θπϕ\nabla_{\theta}\hat{Q}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}} is the influence of changing the cost and model on the simulation-based critic under a fixed policy.

  • •

    ∇ϕQ^θπϕ\nabla_{\phi}\hat{Q}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}} is the influence of changing the policy parameters on the simulation-based critic under a fixed cost and model.

  • •

    ∇ϕ𝔼s∼ρ^θπϕ​[⋅]\nabla_{\phi}\mathbb{E}_{s\sim\hat{\rho}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}}}\left[\cdot\right] is the effect of changing ϕ\phi on the simulation-based distribution ρ^θπϕ\hat{\rho}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}}, and the influence of that change on the expected value under a fixed cost and model.

  • •

    ∇θ𝔼s∼ρ^θπϕ​[⋅]\nabla_{\theta}\mathbb{E}_{s\sim\hat{\rho}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}}}\left[\cdot\right] is the effect of changing θ\theta on the simulation-based distribution ρ^θπϕ\hat{\rho}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}}, and the influence of that change on the expected value under a fixed policy.

From (20):

∇θϕ\displaystyle\nabla_{\theta}\phi =−(𝔼s∼ρ^θπϕ​[∇ϕ​ϕ​log​πϕ​Q^θπϕ+∇ϕ​log​πϕ​∇ϕQ^θπϕ]⏟Gradient​of​φ^​w.r.t.ϕ+∇ϕ𝔼s∼ρ^θπϕ​[∇ϕ​log​πϕ​Q^θπϕ]⏟Gradient​of​dist.ρ^θπϕ​w.r.t.ϕ)−1\displaystyle=-\Bigl(\underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{s\sim\hat{\rho}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}}}\bigl[\nabla_{\phi\phi}\log\pi_{\phi}\,\hat{Q}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}}+\nabla_{\phi}\log\pi_{\phi}\,\nabla_{\phi}\hat{Q}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}}\bigr]}_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathrm{Gradient\,of\,}\hat{\varphi}\mathrm{\,w.r.t.\,}\phi\end{subarray}}\;+\;\underbrace{\nabla_{\phi}\mathbb{E}_{s\sim\hat{\rho}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}}}\bigl[\nabla_{\phi}\log\pi_{\phi}\,\hat{Q}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}}\bigr]}_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathrm{Gradient\,of\,dist.\,}\hat{\rho}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}}\mathrm{\,w.r.t.\,}\phi\end{subarray}}\Bigr)^{-1}
(𝔼s∼ρ^θπϕ​[∇ϕ​log​πϕ​∇θQ^θπϕ]⏟Gradient​of​φ^​w.r.t.θ+∇θ𝔼s∼ρ^θπϕ​[∇ϕ​log​πϕ​Q^θπϕ]⏟Gradient​of​dist.ρ^θπϕ​w.r.t.θ).\displaystyle\qquad\qquad\Bigl(\underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{s\sim\hat{\rho}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}}}\bigl[\nabla_{\phi}\log\pi_{\phi}\,\nabla_{\theta}\hat{Q}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}}\bigr]}_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathrm{Gradient\,of\,}\hat{\varphi}\mathrm{\,w.r.t.\,}\theta\end{subarray}}\;+\;\underbrace{\nabla_{\theta}\mathbb{E}_{s\sim\hat{\rho}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}}}\bigl[\nabla_{\phi}\log\pi_{\phi}\,\hat{Q}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}}\bigr]}_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathrm{Gradient\,of\,dist.\,}\hat{\rho}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}}\mathrm{\,w.r.t.\,}\theta\end{subarray}}\Bigr). (23)

With this, we next unpack the effect of changing ϕ,θ\phi,\theta on the simulation-based distribution ρ^θπϕ\hat{\rho}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}}, and the influence of that change on the expected value. In order to develop that aspect, let us develop the notion of sensitivity over Markov Chains.

A.1 Proof of Lemma 1: Sensitivity over Markov Chains

For compactness, let us consider a generic function η⁡(s,a)\eta\left(s,a\right) of the state and action, and its expected value at a specific time stage kk:

𝔼s∼ρ^θ,kπϕ​[η⁡(sk,ak)]=∫η⁡(sk,ak)​∫ρ0​(s0)​πϕ​(ak|sk)​∏i=0k−1fθ,ϕπ​(si+1,si,ai)​d​si​d​ai​d​sk\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{s\sim\hat{\rho}_{\theta,k}^{\pi_{\phi}}}\left[\eta\left(s_{k},a_{k}\right)\right]=\int\eta\left(s_{k},a_{k}\right)\int\rho^{0}\left(s_{0}\right)\,\pi_{\phi}(a_{k}|s_{k})\prod_{i=0}^{k-1}f^{\pi}_{\theta,\phi}\left(s_{i+1},s_{i},a_{i}\right)\mathrm{d}s_{i}\mathrm{d}a_{i}\mathrm{d}s_{k} (24)

where

fθ,ϕπ​(si+1,si,ai)=fθ​(si+1|si,ai)​πϕ​(ai|si)\displaystyle f^{\pi}_{\theta,\phi}\left(s_{i+1},s_{i},a_{i}\right)=f_{\theta}\left(s_{i+1}|s_{i},a_{i}\right)\pi_{\phi}\left(a_{i}|s_{i}\right) (25)

where fθf_{\theta} is the simulation model (assumed stochastic here), and ρ0\rho^{0} the initial condition distribution, assumed fixed here. Differentiating this expected value w.r.t. ϕ,θ\phi,\theta (assuming Leibniz rule) then reads as (arguments omitted for simplicity):

∂𝔼s∼ρ^θ,kπϕ\displaystyle\partial\mathbb{E}_{s\sim\hat{\rho}_{\theta,k}^{\pi_{\phi}}} [η⁡(sk,ak)]\displaystyle\left[\eta\left(s_{k},a_{k}\right)\right] (26)
=∫η​∫ρ0​∂(πϕ​(ak|sk)​∏i=0k−1fθ,ϕπ)​d​si​d​ai​d​sk\displaystyle=\int\eta\int\rho^{0}\partial\left(\pi_{\phi}\left(a_{k}|s_{k}\right)\prod_{i=0}^{k-1}f^{\pi}_{\theta,\phi}\right)\mathrm{d}s_{i}\mathrm{d}a_{i}\mathrm{d}s_{k}
=∫η​∫ρ0​∂log⁡(πϕ​(ak|sk)​∏i=0k−1fθ,ϕπ)​πϕ​(ak|sk)​∏i=0k−1fθ,ϕπ​d​si​d​ai​d​sk\displaystyle=\int\eta\int\rho^{0}\partial\log\left(\pi_{\phi}\left(a_{k}|s_{k}\right)\prod_{i=0}^{k-1}f^{\pi}_{\theta,\phi}\right)\pi_{\phi}\left(a_{k}|s_{k}\right)\prod_{i=0}^{k-1}f^{\pi}_{\theta,\phi}\mathrm{d}s_{i}\mathrm{d}a_{i}\mathrm{d}s_{k}
=∫η​∫ρ0​(∂log⁡πϕ​(ak|sk)+∑i=0k−1∂log⁡fθ,ϕπ)​πϕ​(ak|sk)​∏i=0k−1fθ,ϕπ​d​si​d​ai​d​sk\displaystyle=\int\eta\int\rho^{0}\left(\partial\log\pi_{\phi}\left(a_{k}|s_{k}\right)+\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}\partial\log f^{\pi}_{\theta,\phi}\right)\pi_{\phi}\left(a_{k}|s_{k}\right)\prod_{i=0}^{k-1}f^{\pi}_{\theta,\phi}\mathrm{d}s_{i}\mathrm{d}a_{i}\mathrm{d}s_{k}

Which has the expected value form:

∂𝔼s∼ρ^θ,kπϕ​[η⁡(sk,ak)]=𝔼s0∼ρ0,ai∼πϕ,si+1∼fθπϕ​[η⁡(sk,ak)​(∂log⁡πϕ​(ak∣sk)+∑i=0k−1∂log⁡fθπϕ)].\displaystyle\partial\,\mathbb{E}_{s\sim\hat{\rho}_{\theta,k}^{\pi_{\phi}}}\bigl[\eta(s_{k},a_{k})\bigr]=\mathbb{E}_{\begin{subarray}{c}s_{0}\sim\rho^{0},\,a_{i}\sim\pi_{\phi},\\ s_{i+1}\sim f^{\pi_{\phi}}_{\theta}\end{subarray}}\Bigl[\,\eta(s_{k},a_{k})\,\Bigl(\partial\log\pi_{\phi}(a_{k}\!\mid\!s_{k})+\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}\partial\log f^{\pi_{\phi}}_{\theta}\Bigr)\Bigr]\,. (27)

Computational aspect

In practice, (27) will be evaluated from a model sampling. Let us label

s0j,a0j,…,sNj,aNj\displaystyle s_{0}^{j},a_{0}^{j},\ldots,s_{N}^{j},a_{N}^{j} (28)

the sampled trajectory j∈{1,…,n}j\in\left\{1,\ldots,n\right\} of length NN. The expected value approximation would then read:

𝔼s∼ρ^θ,kπϕ​[η⁡(sk,ak)]≈1n​∑j=1nη⁡(skj,akj)\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{s\sim\hat{\rho}_{\theta,k}^{\pi_{\phi}}}\left[\eta\left(s_{k},a_{k}\right)\right]\approx\frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\eta\left(s_{k}^{j},a_{k}^{j}\right) (29)

Its sensitivities would then read as:

∂𝔼s∼ρ^θ,kπϕ[η(sk,ak)]≈1n∑j=1nη(skj,akj)⊗(Wkj+∂logπϕ(akj|skj))\displaystyle\partial\mathbb{E}_{s\sim\hat{\rho}_{\theta,k}^{\pi_{\phi}}}\left[\eta\left(s_{k},a_{k}\right)\right]\approx\frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\eta\left(s_{k}^{j},a_{k}^{j}\right)\otimes\left(W^{j}_{k}+\partial\log\pi_{\phi}\left(\left.a_{k}^{j}\right|s_{k}^{j}\right)\right) (30)

where

Wkj=∑i=0k−1∂logfθ,ϕπ(si+1j|sij,aij)\displaystyle W^{j}_{k}=\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}\partial\log f^{\pi}_{\theta,\phi}\left(\left.s^{j}_{i+1}\right|s^{j}_{i},a^{j}_{i}\right) (31)

Note that WkjW^{j}_{k} can be carried forward as a dynamic alongside the model trajectory, i.e.

Wkj=Wk−1j+∂logfθ,ϕπ(skj|sk−1j,ak−1j),W0j=0\displaystyle W^{j}_{k}=W^{j}_{k-1}+\partial\log f^{\pi}_{\theta,\phi}\left(\left.s^{j}_{k}\right|s^{j}_{k-1},a^{j}_{k-1}\right),\quad W^{j}_{0}=0 (32)

Expected value over full Markov Chain

For policy gradient methods, we need to compute objects in the form

𝔼⁡[∑k=0∞η⁡(sk,ak)]≈1n​N​∑k=0N∑j=1nη⁡(skj,akj)\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\eta\left(s_{k},a_{k}\right)\right]\approx\frac{1}{nN}\sum_{k=0}^{N}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\eta\left(s_{k}^{j},a_{k}^{j}\right) (33)

and process their sensitivities. There is no significant difference from Sec. A, i.e. the sensitivities read as:

∂𝔼[∑k=0∞η(sk,ak)]≈1n​N∑k=0N∑j=1nη(skj,akj)⊗(Wkj+∂logπϕ(akj|skj))\displaystyle\partial\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\eta\left(s_{k},a_{k}\right)\right]\approx\frac{1}{nN}\sum_{k=0}^{N}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\eta\left(s_{k}^{j},a_{k}^{j}\right)\otimes\left(W^{j}_{k}+\partial\log\pi_{\phi}\left(\left.a_{k}^{j}\right|s_{k}^{j}\right)\right) (34)

Efforts can be put in computing (34) in the most efficient way in terms of flops and memory requirements, but that may be best left for other people to figure out.

Sensitivity for the policy gradient

We can then provide computational expressions for the policy gradient. We observe that

∇ϕ𝔼s∼ρ^θπϕ[∇ϕlogπϕQ^θπϕ]≈1n​N∑k=0N∑j=1n\displaystyle\nabla_{\phi}\mathbb{E}_{s\sim\hat{\rho}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}}}\left[\nabla_{\phi}\log\pi_{\phi}\,\hat{Q}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}}\right]\approx\frac{1}{nN}\sum_{k=0}^{N}\sum_{j=1}^{n} ∇ϕ​log​πϕ​(skj)​Q^θπϕ​(skj,akj)\displaystyle\nabla_{\phi}\log\pi_{\phi}\left(s_{k}^{j}\right)\,\hat{Q}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}}\left(s_{k}^{j},a_{k}^{j}\right)
⊗(Wϕ,kj+∂logπϕ(akj|skj))\displaystyle\otimes\left(W_{\phi,k}^{j}+\partial\log\pi_{\phi}\left(\left.a_{k}^{j}\right|s_{k}^{j}\right)\right) (35)

where Wϕ,0j=0W^{j}_{\phi,0}=0 and

Wϕ,kj\displaystyle W_{\phi,k}^{j} =Wϕ,k−1j+∇ϕ​log​fθ,ϕπ​(skj,sk−1j,ak−1j)\displaystyle=W_{\phi,k-1}^{j}+\nabla_{\phi}\log f^{\pi}_{\theta,\phi}\left(s^{j}_{k},s^{j}_{k-1},a^{j}_{k-1}\right) (36)
=Wϕ,k−1j+∇ϕlogπϕ(ak−1j|sk−1j)\displaystyle=W_{\phi,k-1}^{j}+\nabla_{\phi}\log\pi_{\phi}\left(\left.a^{j}_{k-1}\right|s^{j}_{k-1}\right)

Similarly

∇θ𝔼s∼ρ^θπϕ[∇ϕlogπϕQ^θπϕ]≈1n​N∑k=0N∑j=1n\displaystyle\nabla_{\theta}\mathbb{E}_{s\sim\hat{\rho}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}}}\left[\nabla_{\phi}\log\pi_{\phi}\,\hat{Q}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}}\right]\approx\frac{1}{nN}\sum_{k=0}^{N}\sum_{j=1}^{n} ∇ϕ​log​πϕ​(skj)​Q^θπϕ​(skj,akj)\displaystyle\nabla_{\phi}\log\pi_{\phi}\left(s_{k}^{j}\right)\,\hat{Q}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}}\left(s_{k}^{j},a_{k}^{j}\right)
⊗(Wθ,kj+∂logπϕ(akj|skj))\displaystyle\otimes\left(W_{\theta,k}^{j}+\partial\log\pi_{\phi}\left(\left.a_{k}^{j}\right|s_{k}^{j}\right)\right) (37)

where Wθ,0j=0W^{j}_{\theta,0}=0 and

Wθ,kj\displaystyle W_{\theta,k}^{j} =Wθ,k−1j+∇θ​log​fθ,ϕπ​(skj,sk−1j,ak−1j)\displaystyle=W_{\theta,k-1}^{j}+\nabla_{\theta}\log f^{\pi}_{\theta,\phi}\left(s^{j}_{k},s^{j}_{k-1},a^{j}_{k-1}\right) (38)
=Wθ,k−1j+∇θlogfθ(skj|sk−1j,ak−1j)\displaystyle=W_{\theta,k-1}^{j}+\nabla_{\theta}\log f_{\theta}\left(\left.s^{j}_{k}\right|s^{j}_{k-1},a^{j}_{k-1}\right)

These terms ought to be added to (22b), (22a) respectively. In implementations, these terms would simply weigh the contributions in forming the policy gradient sensitivities.

A.2 Proof of Lemma 2: Sensitivities of the policy evaluation

The simulation-based critic ideally satisfies the following equations:

Q^θπϕ​(s,a)\displaystyle\hat{Q}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}}\left(s,a\right) =Rθ(s,a)+γ𝔼s+∼fθ[V^θπϕ(s+)|s,a]\displaystyle=R_{\theta}\left(s,a\right)+\gamma\mathbb{E}_{s_{+}\sim f_{\theta}}\left[\left.\hat{V}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}}\left(s_{+}\right)\,\right|\,s,a\right] (39a)
V^θπϕ​(s)\displaystyle\hat{V}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}}\left(s\right) =𝔼a∼πϕ​[Q^θπϕ​(s,a)]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi_{\phi}}\left[\hat{Q}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}}\left(s,a\right)\right] (39b)

To compute the sensitivities “safely", we observe that (39) in full reads as:

Q^θπϕ​(s,a)\displaystyle\hat{Q}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}}\left(s,a\right) =Rθ​(s,a)+γ​∫V^θπϕ​(s+)​fθ​(s+|s,a)​d​s+\displaystyle=R_{\theta}\left(s,a\right)+\gamma\int\hat{V}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}}\left(s_{+}\right)f_{\theta}\left(s_{+}|s,a\right)\mathrm{d}s_{+} (40a)
V^θπϕ​(s)\displaystyle\hat{V}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}}\left(s\right) =∫Q^θπϕ​(s,a)​πϕ​(a|s)​𝑑a\displaystyle=\int\hat{Q}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}}\left(s,a\right)\pi_{\phi}\left(a|s\right)\mathrm{d}a (40b)

Their sensitivities are then given by:

∂Q^θπϕ​(s,a)=\displaystyle\partial\hat{Q}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}}\left(s,a\right)= ∂Rθ​(s,a)+γ​∫∂V^θπϕ​(s+)​fθ​(s+|s,a)​d​s+\displaystyle\,\partial R_{\theta}\left(s,a\right)+\gamma\int\partial\hat{V}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}}\left(s_{+}\right)f_{\theta}\left(s_{+}|s,a\right)\mathrm{d}s_{+}
+γ∫V^θπϕ(s+)fθ(s+|s,a)∂logfθ(s+|s,a)ds+\displaystyle\,+\gamma\int\hat{V}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}}\left(s_{+}\right)f_{\theta}\left(s_{+}|s,a\right)\partial\log f_{\theta}\left(s_{+}|s,a\right)\mathrm{d}s_{+} (41a)
∂V^θπϕ​(s)=\displaystyle\partial\hat{V}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}}\left(s\right)= ∫∂⁡Q^θπϕ​(s,a)​πϕ​(a|s)​𝑑a+∫Q^θπϕ​(s,a)​πϕ​(a|s)​∂log⁡πϕ​(a|s)​𝑑a\displaystyle\,\int\partial\hat{Q}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}}\left(s,a\right)\pi_{\phi}\left(a|s\right)\mathrm{d}a+\int\hat{Q}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}}\left(s,a\right)\pi_{\phi}\left(a|s\right)\partial\log\pi_{\phi}\left(a|s\right)\mathrm{d}a (41b)

In the compact “expected value" format, they then read as:

∂Q^θπϕ​(s,a)=\displaystyle\partial\hat{Q}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}}\left(s,a\right)= ∂Rθ​(s,a)+γ​𝔼s+∼fθ​(s,a)​[∂V^θπϕ​(s+)+V^θπϕ​(s+)​∂log⁡fθ​(s+|s,a)]\displaystyle\;\partial R_{\theta}\left(s,a\right)+\gamma\mathbb{E}_{s_{+}\sim f_{\theta}\left(s,a\right)}\left[\partial\hat{V}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}}\left(s_{+}\right)+\hat{V}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}}\left(s_{+}\right)\partial\log f_{\theta}\left(s_{+}|s,a\right)\right]
∂V^θπϕ​(s)=\displaystyle\partial\hat{V}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}}\left(s\right)= 𝔼a∼πϕ​(a|s)​[∂Q^θπϕ​(s,a)+Q^θπϕ​(s,a)​∂log⁡πϕ​(a|s)]\displaystyle\;\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi_{\phi}\left(a|s\right)}\left[\partial\hat{Q}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}}\left(s,a\right)+\hat{Q}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}}\left(s,a\right)\partial\log\pi_{\phi}\left(a|s\right)\right]

Note that this “format" of sensitivity (QQ and VV split) is possibly best for a critic that has function approximators dedicated to VV and QQ separately (or rather VV and AA).

Sensitivity of the Policy Evaluation w.r.t. θ\theta and ϕ\phi

We want to derive separately the two sensitivities

∇θQ^θπϕand∇ϕQ^θπϕ,\nabla_{\theta}\hat{Q}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}}\quad\text{and}\quad\nabla_{\phi}\hat{Q}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}},

starting from the general (“compact”) policy-evaluation equations (42): Here, each of the two sensitivity questions below assumes that the other parameter is held fixed.

1. Sensitivity w.r.t. θ\theta, keeping ϕ\phi fixed

We want

∇θQ^θπϕ​(s,a)and∇θV^θπϕ​(s).\nabla_{\theta}\hat{Q}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}}(s,a)\quad\text{and}\quad\nabla_{\theta}\hat{V}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}}(s).

Starting from (42):

∇θQ^θπϕ(s,a)=∇θRθ(s,a)+γ𝔼s+∼fθ(⋅∣s,a)[∇θV^θπϕ(s+)+V^θπϕ(s+)∇θlogfθ(s+∣s,a)].\displaystyle\nabla_{\theta}\hat{Q}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}}(s,a)\;=\;\nabla_{\theta}R_{\theta}(s,a)+\gamma\mathbb{E}_{s_{+}\sim f_{\theta}(\cdot\mid s,a)}\Bigl[\nabla_{\theta}\hat{V}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}}(s_{+})+\hat{V}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}}(s_{+})\,\nabla_{\theta}\log f_{\theta}(s_{+}\mid s,a)\Bigr]. (43)

Since, πϕ\pi_{\phi} is fixed w.r.t. θ\theta, hence: ∇θ​log​πϕ​(a∣s)= 0.\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\phi}(a\mid s)\;=\;0. We get

∇θV^θπϕ(s)=𝔼a∼πϕ(⋅∣s)[∇θQ^θπϕ(s,a)].\nabla_{\theta}\hat{V}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}}(s)=\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi_{\phi}(\cdot\mid s)}\bigl[\nabla_{\theta}\hat{Q}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}}(s,a)\bigr]. (44)

These two coupled equations show how to backpropagate the effect of changing θ\theta (the model or cost parameters) under a fixed policy πϕ\pi_{\phi}.

2. Sensitivity w.r.t. ϕ\phi, keeping θ\theta fixed

Now we want

∇ϕQ^θπϕ​(s,a)and∇ϕV^θπϕ​(s),\nabla_{\phi}\hat{Q}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}}(s,a)\quad\text{and}\quad\nabla_{\phi}\hat{V}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}}(s),

with θ\theta fixed. That means

∇ϕ​log​fθ​(s+∣s,a)= 0,\nabla_{\phi}\log f_{\theta}(s_{+}\mid s,a)\;=\;0\,, (45)

and the reward sensitivity is

∇ϕRθ​(s,a)= 0.\nabla_{\phi}R_{\theta}(s,a)\;=\;0\,. (46)

From (42) again:

∇ϕQ^θπϕ​(s,a)=\displaystyle\nabla_{\phi}\hat{Q}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}}(s,a)\;= γ𝔼s+∼fθ(⋅∣s,a)[∇ϕV^θπϕ(s+)],\displaystyle\;\gamma\,\mathbb{E}_{s_{+}\sim f_{\theta}(\cdot\mid s,a)}\Bigl[\nabla_{\phi}\hat{V}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}}(s_{+})\;\Bigr]\,, (47)
∇ϕV^θπϕ​(s)=\displaystyle\nabla_{\phi}\hat{V}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}}(s)\;= 𝔼a∼πϕ(⋅∣s)[∇ϕQ^θπϕ(s,a)+Q^θπϕ(s,a)∇ϕlogπϕ(a∣s)].\displaystyle\;\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi_{\phi}(\cdot\mid s)}\Bigl[\nabla_{\phi}\hat{Q}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}}(s,a)\;+\;\hat{Q}_{\theta}^{\pi_{\phi}}(s,a)\,\nabla_{\phi}\log\pi_{\phi}(a\mid s)\Bigr]. (48)

Here, we iteratively compute the required gradients, ∇θQ^θπϕ,∇θV^θπϕ,∇ϕQ^θπϕ,∇ϕQ^θπϕ\nabla_{\theta}\hat{Q}^{\pi_{\phi}}_{\theta},\nabla_{\theta}\hat{V}^{\pi_{\phi}}_{\theta},\nabla_{\phi}\hat{Q}^{\pi_{\phi}}_{\theta},\nabla_{\phi}\hat{Q}^{\pi_{\phi}}_{\theta}, similar to temporal difference learning in value-based methods. For the illustrative examples, we calculate these values till convergence, but they can be approximated using a generic function approximator for bigger problems.

Appendix B Details on Illustrative Examples

B.1 Example 1: Discrete MDP

We considered a finite MDP with state space 𝒮={0,1,2}\mathcal{S}=\{0,1,2\} and action space 𝒜={0,1}\mathcal{A}=\{0,1\}. The real and model MDP parameters have the following form:

Transition logits

θtrans​[s,a]=[θtrans​[s,a,0],θtrans​[s,a,1],θtrans​[s,a,2]]\theta_{\text{trans}}[s,a]\;=\;\bigl[\theta_{\text{trans}}[s,a,0],\,\theta_{\text{trans}}[s,a,1],\,\theta_{\text{trans}}[s,a,2]\bigr]

so that

P⁡(s′∣s,a)=softmax​(θtrans​[s,a])s′.P(s^{\prime}\!\mid s,a)=\mathrm{softmax}\bigl(\theta_{\text{trans}}[s,a]\bigr)_{s^{\prime}}.

The real-MDP transition logits are

θrealf={[ 0.5,2.0,0.5],[ 1.0,1.5,0.5]⏟s=0,[ 1.0,1.0,1.0],[ 1.5,1.0,0.5]⏟s=1,[ 0.5,1.0,0.1],[ 1.0,0.5,1.0]⏟s=2}.\theta_{\text{real}}^{f}=\bigl\{\,\underbrace{[\,0.5,2.0,0.5],\,[\,1.0,1.5,0.5]}_{s=0},\;\underbrace{[\,1.0,1.0,1.0],\,[\,1.5,1.0,0.5]}_{s=1},\;\underbrace{[\,0.5,1.0,0.1],\,[\,1.0,0.5,1.0]}_{s=2}\,\bigr\}.
R⁡(s,a)=θR​[s,a],R(s,a)=\theta^{R}[s,a],

with

θrealR=[1.00.50.03.00.012.0].\theta_{\text{real}}^{R}=\begin{bmatrix}1.0&0.5\\ 0.0&3.0\\ 0.01&2.0\end{bmatrix}.

A similar structure holds for the simulation MDP, where the simulation model and reward parameters for the trials shown in Figure 3 were initialized at random in [0,5][0,5].

The in-sim policy is solved using dp with a convergence threshold of 1×10−21\times 10^{-2}, which provides a deterministic policy, which is then converted into a stochastic policy. After solving the discrete MDP by soft value iteration, we obtain a state–action value table

Q⋆​(s,a)=R⁡(s,a)+γ​∑s′P⁡(s′∣s,a)​V⋆​(s′),Q^{\star}(s,a)\;=\;R(s,a)\;+\;\gamma\,\sum_{s^{\prime}}P(s^{\prime}\mid s,a)\,V^{\star}(s^{\prime})\,,

where P⁡(s′∣s,a)P(s^{\prime}\!\mid s,a) and R⁡(s,a)R(s,a) come from the MDP parameters. A greedy policy would be

πdet​(s)=arg⁡maxa​Q⋆​(s,a),\pi_{\mathrm{det}}(s)=\arg\max_{a}Q^{\star}(s,a)\,,

but this is non-differentiable. Instead, we define a soft (stochastic) policy

π⁡(a∣s)=exp⁡(Q⋆​(s,a)/τ)∑bexp⁡(Q⋆​(s,b)/τ),\pi(a\mid s)\;=\;\frac{\exp\bigl(Q^{\star}(s,a)/\tau\bigr)}{\sum_{b}\exp\bigl(Q^{\star}(s,b)/\tau\bigr)}\,,

where τ>0\tau>0 is a temperature parameter controlling exploration, which we set as 2.0. Because every entry of π(⋅∣s)\pi(\cdot\mid s) is a smooth function of the underlying Q⋆Q^{\star}, and Q⋆Q^{\star} itself depends differentiably on the simulator parameters θ\theta, this construction makes the whole inner loop fully differentiable.

Once Q⋆Q^{\star} is computed, we set the policy logits as:

logits​(s,a)=log⁡(π⁡(a∣s))⟹π⁡(a∣s)=softmax⁡(logits​(s,⋅)).\text{logits}(s,a)\;=\;\log\bigl(\pi(a\mid s)\bigr)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\pi(a\mid s)=\mathrm{softmax}\bigl(\text{logits}(s,\cdot)\bigr)\,.

Using an on-policy, in-simulation trajectory of length 1000 drawn from the dp solution, we compute the Markov-chain sensitivities (Eq. 15 and 16) and the critic sensitivities (Eq. 13 and 14). Each sensitivity table is represented in tabular form and updated iteratively until convergence with a threshold of 1×10−21\times 10^{-2}. For each outer-level iteration, we use a trajectory of length 1000 generated by applying the in-sim policy to the real mdp to update the model and reward parameters using spg steps according to Eq. (9a) with a learning rate of 0.1.

B.2 Example 2: Continuous MDP

We use a one-dimensional linear system with additive Gaussian noise and an exponential reward:

st+1\displaystyle s_{t+1} =θs​st+θa​at+ϵt,ϵt∼𝒩⁡(0,σ2),\displaystyle=\theta_{s}\,s_{t}\;+\;\theta_{a}\,a_{t}\;+\;\epsilon_{t},\quad\epsilon_{t}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}), (49)
Rθ​(st,at)\displaystyle R_{\theta}(s_{t},a_{t}) =exp⁡(−λ⁡[θq​st2+θr​at2]).\displaystyle=\exp\!\bigl(-\lambda\,[\,\theta_{q}\,s_{t}^{2}+\theta_{r}\,a_{t}^{2}\,]\bigr). (50)

The true system uses θs=θa=θq=θr=1\theta_{s}=\theta_{a}=\theta_{q}=\theta_{r}=1, while all five simulation parameters {θs,θa,θq,θr}\{\theta_{s},\theta_{a},\theta_{q},\theta_{r}\} are initialized uniformly at random in [0,1][0,1].

By taking logarithms of the stage reward, we obtain an equivalent quadratic stage cost c⁡(s,a)=λ⁡(q​s2+r​a2)\,c(s,a)=\lambda\,(q\,s^{2}+r\,a^{2}), with q=θqq=\theta_{q}, r=θrr=\theta_{r}. In the infinite-horizon, γ\gamma-discounted setting, the optimal control law is linear,

at⋆=−K​st,a_{t}^{\star}=-K\,s_{t},

where the gain KK and value-function curvature PP solve the discrete Algebraic Riccati Equation (DARE)

P=λ​q+γ​(θs−θa​K)2​P,K=θa​P​θsr+θa2​P.P=\lambda q+\gamma\,(\theta_{s}-\theta_{a}\,K)^{2}\,P,\qquad K=\frac{\theta_{a}\,P\,\theta_{s}}{r+\theta_{a}^{2}\,P}.

Once PP is found, the optimal value function is V⋆​(s)=P​s2V^{\star}(s)=P\,s^{2} and the greedy policy is a=−K​sa=-K\,s.

To test the robustness of our sensitivity estimates, we fit two small feed-forward nn of one hidden layer of size 6 for the policy and 64 for the value function:

V^ψ​(s)≈V⋆​(s),π^ϕ​(a∣s)≈δ⁡(a+K​s),\hat{V}_{\psi}(s)\approx V^{\star}(s),\qquad\hat{\pi}_{\phi}(a\mid s)\approx\delta(a+K\,s),

where π^ϕ\hat{\pi}_{\phi} is trained to match the exact linear feedback as a stochastic Gaussian policy. The learned V^\hat{V} and π^\hat{\pi} are then used in place of the true LQR quantities in the sensitivity computations inner level.

Using an on-policy, in-simulation trajectory of length 1000 drawn from the approximated nn policy, we compute the Markov-chain sensitivities (Eq. 15 and 16) and the critic sensitivities (Eq. 13 and 14). Sensitivities are computed for each sample until convergence of 1×10−21\times 10^{-2}. For each outer-level iteration, we use 20 trajectories of length 200 generated by applying the in-sim nn approximated policy to the real mdp to update the model and reward parameters using spg steps according to Eq. (9a) with a learning rate of 0.1.
